blocks.text: Have you ever wondered how computers perform arithmetic operations in cryptography? The secret lies in modular arithmetic, a fundamental concept in number theory.

blocks.markdown: In this lesson, we will explore the division algorithm, congruence, and arithmetic modulo $n$. These concepts form the backbone of many cryptographic algorithms and hashing functions.

blocks.title: Division Algorithm
blocks.text: For any integers $a$ and $b$ (with $b > 0$), there exist unique integers $q$ (quotient) and $r$ (remainder) such that $a = bq + r$ and $0 \leq r < b$.

blocks.title: Applying the Division Algorithm
blocks.prompt: Find the quotient and remainder when 23 is divided by 5.
blocks.answer: The quotient is 4 and the remainder is 3.

blocks.markdown: Next, we explore congruence, a concept that allows us to compare integers with respect to a modulus.

blocks.title: Congruence
blocks.text: Two integers $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo $n$ if they have the same remainder when divided by $n$. This is written as $a \equiv b \pmod{n}$.

blocks.title: Checking Congruence
blocks.prompt: Determine if 17 and 5 are congruent modulo 6.

blocks.markdown: Modular arithmetic is a system of arithmetic for integers, where numbers wrap around after reaching a certain value, the modulus.

blocks.title: Modular Arithmetic Operations
blocks.text: Addition and multiplication in modular arithmetic follow the rules: $(a + b) \mod n = ((a \mod n) + (b \mod n)) \mod n$ and $(a \times b) \mod n = ((a \mod n) \times (b \mod n)) \mod n$.

points: The division algorithm provides a way to express any integer as a multiple of another integer plus a remainder.
Congruence modulo $n$ allows comparison of integers based on their remainders.
Modular arithmetic simplifies calculations by wrapping numbers around a modulus.
